message.content:
We don’t have a definitive “largest planet” in the entire universe—our knowledge is limited to what we’ve observed so far. Among the planets we’ve discovered outside our Solar System (exoplanets), the biggest ones are often called “hot Jupiters” and can be several times larger than Jupiter.

**Largest known exoplanets (as of recent surveys)**  
| Exoplanet | Approximate Radius | Approximate Mass | Notes |
|-----------|--------------------|------------------|-------|
| **HD 100546 b** | ~2.5 R<sub>J</sub> | ~10–20 M<sub>J</sub> | A young gas giant orbiting a pre‑main‑sequence star; its size is inferred from direct imaging. |
| **WASP‑17b** | ~1.8 R<sub>J</sub> | ~0.5 M<sub>J</sub> | Extremely inflated due to intense stellar irradiation. |
| **Kepler‑7b** | ~1.9 R<sub>J</sub> | ~0.4 M<sub>J</sub> | One of the lowest‑density planets known. |

These planets are still much smaller than the smallest stars (red dwarfs) and far below the mass threshold that would make them brown dwarfs or stars. In practice, the “largest planet” we can confidently identify is still on the order of a few times Jupiter’s radius, and it remains an active area of research as new telescopes (e.g., JWST, upcoming ground‑based ELTs) continue to discover more massive, inflated worlds.
